# Debate: Four-day work week

- Mode: debate
- Cast: Amara Okafor (prop), Victor Hale (prop), Mei Tanaka-Ruiz (opp)
- Motion: This house would adopt a nationwide four-day work week.

**—**: ROUND 1 · OPENING

**Amara Okafor** [neutral]: The evidence I keep coming back to is that we're already running this experiment and pretending we aren't. Two wards moved to a compressed four-day rota with protected rest days, and burnout dropped by roughly a fifth in twelve weeks, sleep improved, and patient throughput, length of stay and readmissions stayed within normal variation [^1]. Staff told us the guaranteed rest days mattered more than the longer shifts [^1]. That's the whole case in one line: we're not choosing between productivity and rest, we're choosing between planned recovery and collapse. High burnout in our own emergency department went from 29% to 41% in ten months, and nurses are resigning at 14% a year, each replacement costing about four months of salary [^2]. A four-day week, properly designed, is cheaper than the turnover we're already paying for.

**Mei Tanaka-Ruiz** [neutral]: I'll take the wellbeing findings at face value: burnout down roughly a third, sick days down about a fifth [^3]. Fine. But notice who was in the room. Not one pilot covered a hospital, a transport operator or a care home [^4] — the very sectors where a national four-day standard would bite hardest, because a bus still leaves at 7:42 whether or not your team hit its sprint goal [^4]. And even inside the pilots, fewer than half the firms measured output consistently [^3], which means "revenue stayed flat" is doing a lot of unearned work. Managers absorbed the coordination slack, so the gains partly got redistributed, not created [^3]. A mandate nationalises a result we've observed in the easiest fifth of the economy. My case: coverage, measurement, and second-order effects.

**Victor Hale** [neutral]: Kai, before reasons, define your terms, because the opposition's whole case will rest on a bait-and-switch. "Nationwide" means a default standard week set in law, not an identical schedule for every employer, and "adopt" means legislate with a transition, not flip a switch overnight. Three reasons. First, the status quo is itself a policy and must justify itself: it pays for exhaustion in absence, agency fees and resignations, so demand the opposition's number for doing nothing[^5]. Second, we have done this before: the Working Hours Act 1931 made the two-day weekend the default, gave agriculture and shipping a decade and exempted continuous services [^6]. Third, coverage sectors already run on shift rules with rest periods and averaging, so a shorter standard week fits inside that structure, phased by sector and collective agreement. The destination is agreed; now argue about speed.

**—**: ROUND 2 · REBUTTAL

**MODERATOR**: Concrete numbers this round, please. Everyone.

**MODERATOR**: Mei, give us a number. What does this cost?

**Amara Okafor** [thinking]: Mei's strongest point is the unmet need that buses leave on time and wards run 24/7, and she's right that a naive standard week would be unworkable in those sectors. But that's why the reasonable number isn't a flat ten-hour day everywhere, it's a statutory default weekly-hours ceiling with sectoral averaging and continuous-service exemptions, so cover is rostered across the week, not sacrificed to it. On the numbers: 29% burnout in March to 41% by January in our department; six resignations against roughly thirteen expected in our sister site running the same staffing model, at about four months' salary to replace each nurse. That's the cost of doing nothing, and it's already on the books.

**Mei Tanaka-Ruiz** [thinking]: A range, because anyone who gives you one number is selling something. In the nine shift-based organisations that actually held coverage constant, the shorter week needed 18% to 27% more staffed hours, covered by hiring, overtime or agency [^7]. That's the direct cost, and no exemption or averaging formula makes it disappear, it only moves who pays. Two of the nine clawed part of it back within six months through lower sickness and turnover; the other seven didn't measure it [^7]. So call it a net cost in the low-to-mid double digits of payroll for continuous-coverage operations, possibly less where turnover was already brutal. Amara's comparison is one department against one sister site, six resignations against about thirteen expected, which is suggestive but it's n of two. Doing nothing does have a price; it isn't obviously larger than this one.

**Mei Tanaka-Ruiz** [thinking]: Their strongest move is the status-quo-is-also-a-policy line, and it lands: doing nothing does cost money in absence, agency fees and resignations, I won't pretend otherwise. But it cuts both ways, because the same logic says we should count the cost of the mandate, and we mostly can't. Here's the asymmetry: the pilots that produced the impressive wellbeing results were self-selected volunteer firms, overwhelmingly service and knowledge work, and even there fewer than half measured output consistently. Continuous-coverage employers, the ones a national default would actually bind, show 18% to 27% more staffed hours to hold service constant. So the honest comparison isn't "rest versus collapse," it's a measured cost in the sectors we cover badly against an unmeasured saving in the sectors we cover well, then a legal ceiling applied to everyone. That's not a reason to do nothing; it's a reason to sequence, exempt continuous services explicitly, and mandate measurement before mandate. The motion as written nationalises the bet and skips the evidence.

**Victor Hale** [thinking]: Kai, I'll name their strongest point plainly, because it deserves respect: the 18 to 27 percent staffed-hours premium across nine continuous-coverage operations is real, and unlike our wellbeing findings it was measured where coverage was actually held constant. So let me not dodge it. But watch what that number is and is not. It is the cost of covering the same service with fewer hours per worker, in organisations that chose hiring or overtime over reorganisation. It is not the cost of the policy; it is the cost of the most expensive way to implement it. Second, the same nine sites tell you the recovery is load-bearing: two clawed back part of the premium within six months through sickness and turnover alone, and the other seven simply did not measure it, which is an absence of evidence, not evidence of absence. Third, and this is the point Mei cannot answer: her asymmetry argument demands measurement before mandate, yet the status quo runs unmeasured forever. You cannot compare a cost you can see against a saving you refuse to count. Define your terms, then put both columns on the same ledger.

**—**: ROUND 3 · CLOSING

**Amara Okafor** [thinking]: Here's what our own review actually shows: after twelve weeks on the compressed rota, burnout fell 19% and 22% on the two wards, sleep before shifts improved by 40 minutes, and throughput, length of stay and readmissions stayed within normal variation [^8]. The transition premium was 6% more agency hours in the first month, and it fell back to baseline by week eight [^9]. So the measured cost on our side is small, time-limited and quantified, and the measured benefit is large and sustained. Mei's 18 to 27 percent is the cost of covering the same service the most expensive way, hiring or overtime, not the cost of restructuring; and she herself acknowledged two of those nine sites clawed part of it back without even trying [^9]. The honest ledger has a real number on both sides, and ours lands cheaper. What's still open is coverage in continuous-service sectors, and our review says it plainly: the pilot didn't test whole-department round-the-clock cover, and the emergency department proper needs further modelling [^9]. That's exactly why the motion says default and transition, not identical schedules overnight.

**Mei Tanaka-Ruiz** [thinking]: No new arguments, so let me close on the shape of the ledger. Amara's ward numbers are genuine and I'll grant the direction: burnout down around a fifth, sleep up, throughput flat, and a transition premium that faded by week eight. That's a good result in two wards, on a compressed rota, in a department that volunteered for it. Where we still differ is scope, and that gap hasn't closed. Their own review says it didn't test round-the-clock departmental cover and that the emergency department needs further modelling. My 18 to 27 percent came precisely from the nine operations that did hold cover constant, and two of them recovered part of it while seven didn't measure. So one side has a measured benefit in the easy, tested case and an open question where the motion actually binds; the other has a measured cost in exactly that hard case and no comparable benefit evidence. Victor's same-ledger point is fair, and I accept it, but it cuts against the motion as written: a default applied nationwide puts the unmeasured column into law first and models the hard sectors afterwards. Sequence it, exempt continuous services explicitly, mandate measurement, and I'd argue about speed for a decade. Vote against and let the evidence catch up with the ambition.

**Victor Hale** [thinking]: Mei closes by inviting you to sequence, and I accept the invitation precisely because the motion already contains it: national adoption is a default and a transition, not a schedule imposed on Monday. What is genuinely open is round-the-clock cover in continuous-service sectors, and Amara said so plainly; what is not open is the direction of movement in every setting tested. So here is the choice before you. Their side offers to wait for the hard-case model while the easy case keeps costing us resignations we already pay for. Ours offers legislation that sets the default, exempts continuous services explicitly, phases by sector, and mandates the measurement Mei demands, which is the only way the hard case ever gets modelled on purpose rather than by attrition. Nemo dat quod non habet: you cannot get from a policy you refuse to pass the evidence you claim to want. Vote for the motion, and let sequencing be written into the statute.

**—**: ROUND 4 · VERDICT

**—**: STRONGER CASE: OPPOSITION

## Verdict

Stronger case: opp

Both sides scored strongly on evidence and rebuttal, but the Opposition's clarity and persuasion edge reflected a tighter ledger: it granted the wellbeing findings while pressing the unmeasured cost in exactly the sectors the motion binds.

## Sources

[^1]: Meridian Shift Fatigue Review 2025, p. 7. "## 6. The compressed-rota pilot Two wards piloted a compressed rota: four longer days, then three days off."
[^2]: Meridian Shift Fatigue Review 2025, p. 1. "- Staff who slept under six hours before a shift were twice as likely to report a near-miss medication error that week. - Two wards that piloted a compressed rota saw burnout fall by roughly a fifth in twelve weeks, with no loss of patient throughput. - Voluntary nursing resignations reached 14% over the year, and each replacement costs about four months of salary."
[^3]: Four-day week pilot summaries, p. 3. "Workers reported better sleep, more time with family and less stress about household tasks. The improvements appeared within the first two months and held to the end of each pilot. Improvements were smaller for managers, who often absorbed coordination work that had previously been spread across a five-day week."
[^4]: Four-day week pilot summaries, p. 5. "These sectors share a feature that most pilot firms did not: service must be provided at fixed times, whatever happens to productivity. A software team can finish a task faster; a bus still has to leave at 7:42. The pilots therefore tell us a great deal about knowledge work, and much less about the sectors where a national standard would be hardest to apply."
[^5]: Moot court notes, ¶ 2. "¶ 6. Closing options: res ipsa loquitur; "the destination is agreed". Don't sound triumphant. Judges reward conceding a fair point gracefully. ¶ 7. Definitions first. "Nationwide" means the default standard week in law, not an identical schedule for every employer. "Adopt" means legislate a standard with a transition, not switch overnight."
[^6]: Moot court notes, ¶ 1. "Moot court notes: "This house would adopt a nationwide four-day work week" V."
[^7]: Four-day week pilot summaries, p. 6. "The nine were three private clinics, two call centres, two security firms, a hotel group and a logistics depot. In each, managers redesigned rotas rather than hours, and the cost came from covering the hours that productivity gains could not replace."
[^8]: Meridian Shift Fatigue Review 2025, p. 7. "## 6. The compressed-rota pilot Two wards piloted a compressed rota: four longer days, then three days off."
[^9]: Meridian Shift Fatigue Review 2025, p. 8. "## 7. Transition costs The pilot wards needed 6% more agency hours during the transition month to cover handovers. That cost fell back to baseline by week eight, once teams had settled the new handover pattern."
